home.proof.label: What that looks like in practice
home.proof.title: Three examples you won't book anywhere else.
home.proof.card1.title: The raclette hike
home.proof.card1.body: You pick up a raclette kit from a local shop down in the village, then simply walk up the mountain to a hut nobody puts in a brochure. You light the fire yourself.
home.proof.card2.title: The glacier that never closes
home.proof.card2.body: Hintertux is Austria's only year-round ski area. We were still up on the ice cave in June, a group around us, while the rest of the country had long moved to the terrace.
home.proof.card3.title: Five minutes by bus
home.proof.card3.body: The hotels right by the lift are twice as expensive as the ones five minutes away by bus, and you don't know that when you book for the first time. We do.
home.teambuilding.label: Creative partner
home.teambuilding.title: A week that keeps working after the mountain.
home.teambuilding.intro: We work with Kamp Vuur. Not as a loose add-on we bolt on, but as a creative partner who thinks with us about how a week on the mountain can also shift how a team works together.
home.teambuilding.introSecondary: Kamp Vuur builds on the moments that are already there: arrival, the gondola up, dinner, departure day. No obligatory exercise, no flip chart. More an approach that runs invisibly through the week and stays noticeable afterwards.
home.teambuilding.partner.quote: No standard teambuilding or classic training, but unique, experience-based programmes that push a little and put your most important muscle to work: curiosity.

about.story.title: It started on a chairlift.
about.story.p1: SlopeWorks started with a simple observation: the best conversations with colleagues don't happen in meeting rooms. They happen on the chairlift, on the summit, and over a lunch that runs much longer than planned.
about.story.p2: Something shifts when a team is away from the office. Titles matter less, people say what they actually think. We didn't want to leave that to chance, so we built a company around it.
about.story.p3: We organise corporate ski trips for teams of 15 to 40 people in Austria and Switzerland. Every area we propose, we've skied ourselves. We arrange all of it; you just show up and ski.

privacy.title: Privacy statement
privacy.subtitle: How SlopeWorks handles your personal data.
privacy.intro.p1: SlopeWorks BV, registered at Rodekruisstraat 64/1, 3920 Lommel, company number BE 1036.649.787 (hereinafter “SlopeWorks”, “we” or “us”), is the controller for the personal data processed via
privacy.intro.p2: and in the context of our services. This statement explains which data we collect, why, and what rights you have.
privacy.collect.title: What data we collect
privacy.collect.item1: Via the contact form: name, email address, subject and your message.
privacy.collect.item2: For a concrete retreat enquiry: name, job title, company name, contact details and the wishes you share with us (group size, dates, budget, destination).
privacy.collect.item3: If it leads to a booking: the data needed to organise and run the trip, such as participants’ names, insofar as we receive them from the client.
privacy.purpose.title: Why we process this data
privacy.purpose.item1: To respond to your enquiry and prepare a tailored proposal (legitimate interest / pre-contractual step).
privacy.purpose.item2: To perform an agreement with you or your employer, once there is a booking (performance of a contract).
privacy.purpose.item3: To comply with legal obligations, for example the accounting retention requirement for invoices.
privacy.retention.title: Retention period
privacy.retention.body: Contact enquiries that do not lead to a booking are kept for a maximum of 2 years after the last contact. Data from an ongoing or completed booking is kept for as long as needed to carry out the trip and for the statutory accounting retention period thereafter.
privacy.sharing.title: Who we share data with
privacy.sharing.body: Only with partners that are necessary to carry out the trip, such as the hotel, and with Kamp Vuur when a programme element is arranged with them, and always limited to what is needed (for example a participant list). We do not sell data to third parties.
privacy.transfer.title: Transfers outside the EEA
privacy.transfer.body: At present SlopeWorks processes personal data exclusively via email. No other tools, such as a CRM integration or analytics, that process personal data of website visitors are in use. If SlopeWorks uses an email provider outside the EEA, that processing generally takes place under a recognised safeguard (such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework for American providers). As soon as SlopeWorks deploys new tools that process personal data, this statement will be updated.
privacy.storage.title: Cookies and local storage
privacy.storage.body: The website places no tracking or analytics cookies. We only store a single technical preference locally in your browser, namely your language choice, so the site is shown in the right language. This data stays on your device and is not sent to us. You can clear it at any time via your browser settings.
privacy.rights.title: Your rights
privacy.rights.p1: You have the right to access, rectify or erase your data. You can also object to the processing, or ask us to restrict it. Would you like to exercise these rights? Email us at
privacy.complaint.title: Right to complain
privacy.complaint.p1: Are you unhappy with how we handle your data? Let us know first, we are happy to resolve it together. You also have the right to lodge a complaint with the Data Protection Authority, Drukpersstraat 35, 1000 Brussels,

solden.day.label: A sample day
solden.day.title: From first lift to last run in Sölden
solden.day.body: Most groups start around half past eight at the Gaislachkoglbahn, when the pistes are freshly groomed and it's still quiet. We make sure the lift passes are ready and that anyone who hasn't skied in a while can ease into the morning with an instructor. Around midday we eat on the mountain, not down in the valley, so the group stays together. In the afternoon the stronger skiers and the calmer group often split, each at their own pace, before meeting again for the last run down to the village. Anyone done skiing will find plenty in Sölden for a drink or the sauna. In the evening we eat together, usually at the hotel or a spot we've tried ourselves. No rigid schedule, just a day that works.
solden.logistics.label: The logistics
solden.logistics.title: From airport to piste, sorted
solden.logistics.body: For Sölden, groups usually fly into Innsbruck; from there the transfer is about 75 minutes by a coach we arrange, so no one has to drive or change over. The village stretches along the Ötztal, with most hotels within walking or ski-bus distance of the two main lifts. We pick accommodation close enough to the lift that the morning doesn't start with a trek. Skis, boots and passes are sorted in advance, so the first morning isn't a queue at the rental desk. And if the programme runs beyond the piste, a longer lunch or a later start, the rest shifts to match. That's exactly the kind of work we take off your hands.

solden.faq.title: Sölden for corporate trips
solden.faq.q1: Is Sölden suitable for a group with mixed skiing levels?
solden.faq.a1: The area is strongest for teams that can mostly already ski. For groups where more than half have never been on skis, we'd sooner recommend Mayrhofen or Zell am See.
solden.faq.q2: What does a corporate trip to Sölden cost on average per person?
solden.faq.a2: That depends on the number of days, the accommodation and the programme. Because we don't sell fixed packages, we build the price around what your team needs.
solden.faq.q3: When is the best time to take a company to Sölden?
solden.faq.a3: December through April. Thanks to the glacier, snow certainty is high even early and late in the season, when other areas are less reliable.
solden.faq.q4: How far is Sölden from the airport?
solden.faq.a4: From Innsbruck the transfer is about 75 minutes. That's the airport we use for this area.

faq.title: FAQ about your corporate ski trip.
faq.subtitle: Before you book a call, here are the answers to the questions HR and office managers ask us most.
faq.werk.title: How it works
faq.werk.sub: What sets SlopeWorks apart from a travel agency or booking portal.
faq.werk.q1: What makes SlopeWorks different from a travel agency or a corporate-wintersport specialist?
faq.werk.a1: We don't book from a fixed catalogue. We work with a limited number of groups per season, in areas we've been to ourselves, with hotel owners we know by name. No fixed programme that's the same for every group, a proposal that starts with a conversation about your team.
faq.werk.q2: What does the process look like from first contact?
faq.werk.a2: You tell us what you're looking for: group size, dates, budget, and what kind of team it is. Then we put together one proposal, not three packages to choose between. Once agreed, we arrange accommodation, transport, ski pass and programme, with one point of contact through to the last day.
faq.werk.q3: Do you also work with a team coach or facilitator?
faq.werk.a3: For teams that want it, we work with Kamp Vuur. It's not a bolt-on we add to every trip, but something we factor into how we build the programme, based on what the team needs.
faq.prijs.title: Pricing and budget
faq.prijs.sub: What a corporate ski trip costs on average and how we build up prices.
faq.prijs.q1: What does a corporate ski trip cost on average per person?
faq.prijs.a1: That depends on destination, duration and programme. We don't work with fixed entry prices you have to top up later. Based on what your team needs, we put together one complete proposal, including accommodation, ski pass, local transport and dinners.
faq.prijs.q2: Are there hidden costs in a SlopeWorks proposal?
faq.prijs.a2: No. The proposal you receive is the amount you pay. What's included is fixed in advance, so you can defend it internally without surprises afterwards.
faq.prijs.q3: Can I request a quote with no obligation?
faq.prijs.a3: Yes. The first conversation is without obligation. We want to know what your team needs before we propose anything, not the other way around.
faq.groep.title: Groups and level
faq.groep.sub: Who a SlopeWorks trip suits, and who it doesn't.
faq.groep.q1: What group size does SlopeWorks organise trips for?
faq.groep.a1: Usually between 15 and 40 people. That's the group size where we can keep building a tailored programme without it becoming a large, impersonal coach trip.
faq.groep.q2: Is a SlopeWorks trip suitable if not everyone can ski?
faq.groep.a2: Yes, in most areas we build a dedicated programme for non-skiers, so nobody spends a day alone at the hotel. Some destinations, like Sölden, do lean more toward teams that mostly already have skiing experience.
faq.groep.q3: Can a group with mixed levels still travel together?
faq.groep.a3: Yes. We build the programme by level, from first time on skis to experienced skier, so nobody has to wait for anyone and the group still ends the day together.
faq.best.title: Destinations
faq.best.sub: Which areas we offer and how to choose.
faq.best.q1: Which countries does SlopeWorks organise ski trips in?
faq.best.a1: We're active in Austria and Switzerland. France is not part of our offering.
faq.best.q2: Which ski area suits our team best?
faq.best.a2: That depends on the group's level, the budget and what you want to experience. Have a look at the destinations page for an overview, or tell us about your team and we'll think along.
faq.best.q3: What's the difference between the areas SlopeWorks offers?
faq.best.a3: Sölden is sporty and glacier-sure, Mayrhofen is energetic with room for non-skiers, St. Anton has a serious reputation for its pistes, Kitzbühel is well-known and polished, Zell am See is quieter than it looks on paper, and Gstaad sits a tier above the rest in price and refinement.
faq.prakt.title: Practical matters
faq.prakt.sub: Planning, timing and what we need from you.
faq.prakt.q1: When should we book for the ski season?
faq.prakt.a1: The earlier the better for choice of accommodation and dates. For the busier high-season weeks we recommend planning at least four to six months ahead.
faq.prakt.q2: Does SlopeWorks also arrange transport to the ski area?
faq.prakt.a2: We arrange local transport, such as transfers from the airport. The journey to the destination itself we agree on per request.
faq.prakt.q3: What happens if someone drops out at the last minute?
faq.prakt.a3: We discuss that upfront in the cancellation terms, so there's no ambiguity if it happens. Where possible we build in flexibility so a single drop-out doesn't immediately add costs for the group.
faq.cta.title: Not seeing your question?
faq.cta.sub: Send us a message. No sales pitch, just an honest answer.
comparison.title: SlopeWorks compared to an ordinary travel agency.
comparison.subtitle: There are roughly two kinds of provider you meet when looking for a corporate ski trip. Here we explain how SlopeWorks relates to them, without a sales pitch.
comparison.runs.label: The three routes
comparison.runs.title: Three ways down the same mountain
comparison.runs.lead: One mountain, three lines down. Which route suits you depends on your team, your budget and how hands-on you want to be, not on which is 'best'.
comparison.deep.label: The long read
comparison.glance.type.g: Broad tour operator, also sun and family holidays
comparison.glance.strength.u: Knowledge of the area from first-hand experience
comparison.dd1.title: Why people look for an alternative
comparison.dd1.p1: Most companies organising a ski trip run into the same problem. Someone has to do it on top of their own job, and booking a package is quickly done, but it often feels like a standard trip with a different logo on it. The organiser mostly hears afterwards about the things that weren't quite right: the hotel that was further from the lift than expected, the restaurant that couldn't handle a group of twenty.
comparison.dd1.p2: That's no reproach to the existing providers. Both types do what they promise, at scale and with plenty of experience. It's a different choice: scale and convenience, or a smaller, personal approach.
comparison.dd2.title: The generalist: sharp prices, broad offering
comparison.dd2.p1: Some providers are first and foremost a holiday tour operator. Wintersport group trips are then one part of a broader offering that also includes sun holidays and family trips. With hundreds of destinations and a strong negotiating position with ski areas, the strength lies in price and choice, not in specialisation in corporate trips.
comparison.dd2.p2: For a company mostly watching its budget, with little need for a tailored programme, that's a logical choice. For a team looking for an experience that fits their own culture, such a generalist package offers little to hold on to.
comparison.dd3.title: The specialist: a strong, repeatable operation
comparison.dd3.p1: Other providers have devoted themselves entirely to corporate wintersport, at a scale that commands respect: hundreds of companies and thousands of participants a year, often with well-known names as clients. A booking portal and app keep the process tightly organised, and every group gets a fixed contact.
comparison.dd3.p2: That scale has another side. This kind of provider works with a select number of fixed destinations and a programme tuned per sector, but always within a fixed structure. A strong choice for a company seeking a reliable, repeatable experience. For a team that wants something not every other client experiences that season too, it's less distinctive.
comparison.dd4.title: SlopeWorks: smaller, but from first-hand experience
comparison.dd4.p1: SlopeWorks deliberately chooses a different starting point. Rather than scaling to thousands of participants, we work with a limited number of groups per season. Every area we propose (Sölden, Mayrhofen, St. Anton, Kitzbühel, Zell am See or Gstaad) we've visited ourselves. We know the hotel owners by name and know which restaurant can serve a group of twenty without compromising on quality.
comparison.dd4.p2: That also means an honest limitation: we can't send a quote within 48 hours the way a large specialist can, and we're not the cheapest option. What we do offer is a programme built around a specific team, with knowledge that doesn't come from a catalogue.
comparison.who.g.title: Choose a generalist if
comparison.who.g.body: Budget is the most important factor, you want to book quickly without much coordination, and a standard programme works for the group.
comparison.who.s.title: Choose a specialist if
comparison.who.s.body: You have a large group, want a fully automated process via a booking portal, and a proven, repeatable approach matters more than bespoke work.
comparison.who.u.title: Choose SlopeWorks if
comparison.who.u.body: Your team is between 15 and 40 people, you want a programme that fits who you are, and you value a provider that knows the area itself rather than from a database.
comparison.three.label: In detail
comparison.three.title: Three questions that decide the choice

gstaad.subtitle: Swiss, stylish and never rushed.

gstaad.intro1: Gstaad is the exception in our range, and not merely an expensive one. Where the other destinations already sit above average, Gstaad takes that to another level. It has long been a region for those who have time and needn't think about the cost, and you see that in everything, from the hotels to the après-ski.
gstaad.intro2: It is rarely busy. Not everyone who visits comes for the slopes, and only after fresh snow at the weekend, when locals arrive from Thun and the surrounding area, does it get a little fuller. The area is also surprisingly well suited to beginners: plenty of blue runs, gentle descents through the trees and an atmosphere that isn't about performance.

gstaad.signature.title: The raclette walk.
gstaad.signature.body: You collect a raclette kit yourself from a little shop in the village, walk up the mountain to a hut that appears in no brochure, and light the fire yourself. Nobody arranges it for you. No guide, no group activity, no programme. That is exactly why it works, and why people are still talking about it months later.

gstaad.day.label: A sample day
gstaad.day.title: From a slow start to a long lunch in Gstaad
gstaad.day.body: Gstaad is in no hurry, and a day with your team looks the same way. Most groups start a little later than elsewhere, with coffee before we head up the mountain, towards Saanenmöser or Glacier 3000, say. The terrain is broad and calm, suited to almost every level, with plenty of room to ride at your own pace. Anyone on skis for the first time builds the morning up with an instructor. Lunch here isn't a pit stop but part of the programme; we eat at length on the mountain, with a view. In the afternoon we ski on or drift gently back down to the village. In the evening we eat together at a spot we've tried ourselves. No rigid schedule, just a day that takes its time.
gstaad.logistics.label: The logistics
gstaad.logistics.title: From Geneva, across the Swiss countryside
gstaad.logistics.body: For Gstaad, groups usually fly into Geneva; from there the transfer is about two and a half hours by a coach we arrange, so no one has to drive or change over. It's the longest transfer of our six destinations, but the drive through the Swiss countryside is part of the experience. The village is compact and largely car-free, with most hotels within walking distance of the train or the lifts. We pick accommodation close enough to the piste that the morning doesn't start with a trek. Skis, boots and passes are sorted in advance, so the first morning isn't a queue at the rental desk. That's exactly the kind of work we take off your hands.

gstaad.faq.title: Gstaad for company trips
gstaad.faq.a1: Yes, it is one of the most beginner-friendly areas in our range. Plenty of blue runs, gentle descents through the trees and an atmosphere that isn't about performance. Ideal for mixed teams.
gstaad.faq.q2: Who is SlopeWorks' hotel partner in Gstaad?
gstaad.faq.a2: The Golfhotel in Saanenmöser, confirmed. A hotel whose character suits the quiet, stylish nature of the destination.
gstaad.faq.q3: How small can a group be for Gstaad?
gstaad.faq.a3: We run trips here from eight people upwards. The small scale of the destination actually suits a smaller party.
gstaad.faq.q4: How far is Gstaad from the airport?
gstaad.faq.a4: About two and a half hours from Geneva. Bern is an alternative that is slightly closer. The train is also a good option here.

mayrhofen.subtitle: Energetic, affordable and broader than it first appears.

mayrhofen.intro1: Mayrhofen is the area you'd expect to be a quiet, traditional Tyrolean destination, yet it feels calmer than its après-ski reputation suggests. The village has grown through tourism, with a newer centre where the larger hotels define the streetscape, but the old village core is still intact. That is where you still feel the real Tyrol.
mayrhofen.intro2: Two ski areas of its own, Ahorn and Penken, both reachable from the village by gondola. Snow reliability is good from December through March, and if in doubt the Hintertux Glacier is a twenty-minute, direct fallback that stays open all year. Something most groups don't have on their radar.

mayrhofen.signature.title: On the glacier in June. It's entirely possible.
mayrhofen.signature.body: The Hintertux Glacier is Austria's only year-round ski area, twenty minutes from Mayrhofen. We were still standing on the ice cave there in June, with a group around us. Not by chance, but as an option for anyone wanting to organise something outside the usual season, or simply to show that this exists.

mayrhofen.day.label: A sample day
mayrhofen.day.title: From first lift to the dinner table in Mayrhofen
mayrhofen.day.body: Most groups start in the valley and take the Penkenbahn up the mountain, where the terrain is broad enough for beginners and stronger skiers to each find their pace. Anyone on skis for the first time builds the morning up with an instructor; the rest go ahead and explore. Around midday we eat on the mountain, so the group stays together. In the afternoon there's room for those who want to push on and those taking it easy. Later everyone drops back down to the village, where the old centre is still intact for a drink away from the crowd. In the evening we eat together, usually at the hotel or a spot we've tried ourselves. No rigid schedule, just a day that works for everyone.
mayrhofen.logistics.label: The logistics
mayrhofen.logistics.title: Into Innsbruck, on the piste in just over an hour
mayrhofen.logistics.body: For Mayrhofen, groups usually fly into Innsbruck; from there the transfer is about 65 minutes by a coach we arrange, so no one has to drive or change over. The village sits compactly in the Zillertal, with the lifts within walking or ski-bus distance of most hotels. We pick accommodation close enough to the lift that the morning doesn't start with a trek. Skis, boots and passes are sorted in advance, so the first morning isn't a queue at the rental desk. And if the programme runs beyond the piste, a longer lunch or a trip up to the Hintertux glacier, the rest shifts to match. That's exactly the kind of work we take off your hands.
mayrhofen.related.label: Other destinations
mayrhofen.related.title: Have a look at these areas too
mayrhofen.faq.title: Mayrhofen for company trips
mayrhofen.faq.q1: Is Mayrhofen suitable if not everyone can ski?
mayrhofen.faq.a1: Yes. Both ski areas, Ahorn and Penken, have plenty of blue runs for beginners. On top of that, the Hintertux Glacier always offers an alternative for anyone who would rather do something else at altitude.
mayrhofen.faq.q2: Who are SlopeWorks' hotel partners in Mayrhofen?
mayrhofen.faq.a2: In Mayrhofen we work with two hotels at different price levels, so the proposal always matches the budget. Which hotel we suggest is something we discuss in the intake conversation.
mayrhofen.faq.q3: When is the best time to book Mayrhofen for a group?
mayrhofen.faq.a3: December through March, with the peak of the season in January and February. If you want fewer crowds, early December or the weeks after carnival are the better choice.
mayrhofen.faq.q4: How far is Mayrhofen from the airport?
mayrhofen.faq.a4: Around 65 minutes from Innsbruck. The route runs through the wide, gradually rising Zillertal, with no hairpin bends on the final kilometres.

stanton.subtitle: One of the strongest ski areas in the Alps, with no compromises.

stanton.intro1: St. Anton sits within Ski Arlberg, one of the most snow-sure regions in the Alps. The Arlberg massif catches snow from both the north and the west, and the villages lie relatively high. For advanced skiers it is one of the strongest areas you can choose: challenging, steep pistes, few flat stretches, and off-piste options that will keep you busy for seasons.
stanton.intro2: Prices sit clearly above average, both for accommodation and for eating on the mountain. That makes St. Anton the stronger choice for smaller groups: the higher price level and the pronounced character of the destination work better with fifteen to twenty-five people than with large teams.

stanton.signature.body: The name Arlberg means something, even to someone who rarely skis. That makes a trip to St. Anton a different conversation from the start than 'we're going skiing'. We have made contact with Die Arlbergerin, a hotel with a story of its own in the village, which opens up a side of St. Anton you won't find simply by booking a room.

stanton.day.label: A sample day
stanton.day.title: From first descent to last run in St. Anton
stanton.day.body: St. Anton is an area for teams that want to ski, and you notice it first thing in the morning. Most groups start early at the Galzigbahn, when the pistes are still empty and freshly groomed. For a mostly experienced group we keep the day on the skis as much as possible; the steep descents of the Arlberg massif are exactly what you come here for. Around midday we eat on the mountain, so no one has to drop down to regroup. In the afternoon the strongest skiers often head off-piste, with a guide, while the rest ride the well-known runs. In the evening we eat together in the village, where after a day of serious skiing the mood takes care of itself. No rigid schedule, just a day full of vertical metres.
stanton.logistics.label: The logistics
stanton.logistics.title: From Innsbruck, by coach right into the village
stanton.logistics.body: For St. Anton, groups usually fly into Innsbruck; from there the transfer is about 100 minutes by a coach we arrange, so no one has to drive or change over. The village is largely car-free and strung out along the valley, with most hotels within walking distance of the lifts. We pick accommodation close enough to the gondola that the morning doesn't start with a trek. Skis, boots and passes are sorted in advance, so the first morning isn't a queue at the rental desk. Off-piste days with a guide we arrange ahead of time, since they need space and the right kit. That's exactly the kind of work we take off your hands.

stanton.faq.title: St. Anton am Arlberg for company trips
stanton.faq.q1: Is St. Anton suitable for beginners?
stanton.faq.a1: Less so. The area soon asks for more ability than a first or second ski holiday offers. For mixed groups with many beginners we recommend Mayrhofen or Kitzbühel.
stanton.faq.q2: Who is SlopeWorks' hotel partner in St. Anton?
stanton.faq.a2: Die Arlbergerin, confirmed. That contact opens up a side of the village behind the well-known après-ski name.
stanton.faq.q3: How large can a group be in St. Anton?
stanton.faq.a3: We keep it to fifteen to twenty-five people. The higher price level and the smaller restaurants in the village make larger groups harder to organise without compromising on quality.
stanton.faq.q4: How far is St. Anton from the airport?
stanton.faq.a4: Around 100 minutes from Innsbruck. Zurich is an alternative via the Arlberg tunnel, a little further but perfectly doable.

kitzbuhel.intro1: Kitzbühel-Kirchberg has no dramatic high-alpine terrain, but it does offer plenty of varied descents, each with a different view. It is an excellent area for mixed teams: blue runs and a beginners' area for those starting out, with enough challenge for the more advanced who have the famous Streif on their list.
kitzbuhel.intro2: Snow reliability is good despite the low elevation. The grassy mountains lend themselves well to snow cannons, and only a thin layer of snow is needed to ski. That makes the area less dependent on the weather than its altitude might suggest.

Most groups start together at the Hahnenkammbahn and then split by level: beginners build the morning up in the children's area and on the blue runs, while stronger skiers head for the varied descents, with the famous Streif on the list for those who want it. Around midday we regroup on the mountain to eat, so the group stays as one. In the afternoon everyone rides at their own pace, with a different view around each corner. Anyone done skiing finds plenty in town for a drink. In the evening we eat together, usually at the hotel or a spot we've tried ourselves. No rigid schedule, just a day that works for every level.

Kitzbühel and Kirchberg sit close together, with most hotels within walking or ski-bus distance of the lifts. We pick accommodation close enough to the gondola that the morning doesn't start with a trek. Skis, boots and passes are sorted in advance, so the first morning isn't a queue at the rental desk. And if the programme runs beyond the piste, a longer lunch or an afternoon in town, the rest shifts to match. That's exactly the kind of work we take off your hands.

kitzbuhel.faq.title: Kitzbühel-Kirchberg for company trips
kitzbuhel.faq.a1: Yes, it is one of the better areas for mixed teams. There are plenty of blue runs and beginners' areas across several sectors, and the atmosphere is less overtly sporty than in St. Anton or Sölden.
kitzbuhel.faq.q2: Where is best for a group dinner in Kitzbühel-Kirchberg?
kitzbuhel.faq.a2: That depends on the size of the group. The village of Kitzbühel has atmospheric places to eat but is small in scale. Kirchberg offers more room for larger groups. We know the places that can handle a group of twenty.
kitzbuhel.faq.q3: How far is Kitzbühel from the airport?
kitzbuhel.faq.a3: About 75 minutes from Innsbruck. Salzburg is an alternative at a comparable distance.

zellamsee.subtitle: Lake and mountain in one, cosmopolitan and broadly suitable.

zellamsee.intro1: Zell am See sits right on the lake of the same name and pairs that with direct access to the slopes. The village can feel a little urban for a ski area, with more to do off the piste than at most other destinations. Kaprun lies close by as an extension, with the Kitzsteinhorn glacier reaching up to 3,029 metres.
zellamsee.intro2: Timing here is specific: December and the early spring, the start of March or April, are the best moments for a group looking for calm. January is the busiest time and works less well for a team that wants a bit more space. The restaurants in the centre are generally small; for groups of twenty or more, Kaprun is the better choice for evening programmes.

zellamsee.signature.title: The lake makes the difference.
zellamsee.signature.body: At most ski destinations you look up into the mountain. Here you also look down into the valley, over the lake, with a view that on a clear day reaches across the Hohe Tauern. We have access here to corners of the valley that aren't in the standard brochure, including spots on the mountain that, for a group dinner, make the difference between an ordinary evening out and something that stays with you.

zellamsee.day.body: Zell am See-Kaprun gives you two mountains and a lake, and that keeps the day flexible. Most groups start on the Schmittenhöhe, right above the village, where the terrain suits almost every level. Anyone on skis for the first time builds the morning up with an instructor; the rest explore the runs looking out over the lake. Around midday we eat on the mountain, so the group stays together. If part of the group wants higher, more snow-sure terrain, the Kitzsteinhorn glacier at Kaprun is an afternoon trip. Later there's plenty to do off the piste in the village, more than at most destinations. In the evening we eat together at a spot we've tried ourselves. No rigid schedule, just a day with options.

The village sits right on the lake, with most hotels within walking or ski-bus distance of the Schmittenhöhe and the link to Kaprun. We pick accommodation close enough to the lift that the morning doesn't start with a trek. Skis, boots and passes are sorted in advance, so the first morning isn't a queue at the rental desk. And if the programme runs beyond the piste, an afternoon by the lake or a trip to the glacier, the rest shifts to match. That's exactly the kind of work we take off your hands.

zellamsee.faq.a1: December and the weeks from early March to April are the better moments. January is the busiest and most touristy time, less suitable for a group looking for calm.
zellamsee.faq.q2: Can we eat in the centre with a large group?
zellamsee.faq.a2: Most restaurants in the centre of Zell am See are relatively small. For groups of twenty or more, Kaprun is the better choice for evening programmes with the whole group together.
zellamsee.faq.q3: How far is Zell am See from the airport?
zellamsee.faq.a3: About 80 minutes from Salzburg. That is the nearest airport and the most logical route in.
